drapeaux.note: The two creed passages are copied word for word from the English text of the Nicene Creed of 325 in the Percival translation (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, vol. 14) on Wikisource, the address already listed in the French sources: “begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father” and “there was a time when the Son of God was not” (from “whosoever shall say that there was a time when the Son of God was not”). The Greek words that the source prints in parentheses inside these phrases are left out of the quotations; “homoousios” is added after the first quotation, as in the French.

titre: At Nicaea in 325, Orthodoxy Is Decided Within Two Votes
accroche: 318 bishops are said to have settled the nature of Christ with all but two in agreement. A direct witness counted only about 250.
contenu_vulgarise:
In May 325, Emperor Constantine summons bishops from all over the Roman Empire to Nicaea, at his own expense. He has only recently come to rule a unified territory, and has just discovered that a theological question (is the Son of God of the same nature as the Father, or only a superior creature, created by him?) is dividing his new eastern provinces to the point of threatening the civil peace he is trying to impose. For several weeks, in the hall of the imperial palace, more than two hundred bishops debate a question that no earlier text had settled unambiguously.

## A Vote, Not a Revelation

The council arrives at a text, the Nicene Creed, which affirms the Son as “begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father” (homoousios) and condemns those who maintain “there was a time when the Son of God was not.” Yet the Greek term homoousios was not a given before the debates opened: Eusebius of Caesarea, who was himself present, attributes it in a letter to his own flock to the personal intervention of Constantine, who at the time was not even baptized. Of all the participants, three refuse to sign the final text: Arius, a mere priest whose doctrine is condemned, and two bishops who remain loyal to him, Theonas and Secundus, who are immediately exiled with him.

The exact number of participants has remained uncertain. Eusebius, a direct witness, counts about 250. The figure of 318, which stuck throughout the later tradition, appears only decades later, in Athanasius. It received, as early as Antiquity, a reading that is nothing like a simple headcount: Ambrose of Milan links this number to the 318 servants Abraham arms to rescue Lot, in Genesis; in Greek numeration, where each letter is worth a number, 318 is written tau-iota-eta, a tau that draws a cross and an iota-eta that abbreviates the name of Jesus. The historian Philip Schaff, in the 19th century, suggests that the number of members may have grown toward the end of the council, so that Eusebius and Athanasius could each be right.

## What This Changes

None of this implies that the Nicene Creed is arbitrary or lacks earlier theological grounding: the question it settles had been debated for decades. But what later generations receive as a stable truth, handed down from time immemorial, was in 325 a real disagreement, carried by an overwhelming majority rather than by unanimity, under the pressure of an emperor as concerned with the unity of his empire as with theological correctness. And the very figure by which this council has long been summed up, 318 bishops, owes its stability to its symbolic weight at least as much as to a verified count. What history retains of an agreement does not always coincide with what was actually discussed in the room.

repere.texte: Eusebius of Caesarea, who was present at the council, counts about 250 bishops at Nicaea in 325. The figure of 318, fixed by Athanasius decades later and kept in the tradition, is also worth 318 in Greek numeration (tau-iota-eta) and was linked by Ambrose of Milan to the 318 servants of Abraham in Genesis (14:14).
repere.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. III, 1867; First Council of Nicaea, Wikipedia

carte.punch: 318 bishops are said to have settled the nature of Christ. The number itself is a symbol.
carte.idee: At the Council of Nicaea in 325, only Arius and two bishops refuse to sign the text on the nature of Christ. But the number kept in the tradition, 318, owes as much to a symbolic reading (Greek numeration, Genesis 14:14) as to a real headcount: a direct witness counted only about 250.

quiz.question: Why is the figure of 318 bishops present at Nicaea misleading?
choix: Because a direct witness counted about 250, long before 318 took hold
Because no bishop actually took part in the council, only deacons
Because the council was never held at Nicaea but at Constantinople
Because Constantine forbade any official count of those present
quiz.explication: Eusebius of Caesarea, who was present at the council, speaks of about 250 bishops; the figure of 318, fixed by Athanasius decades later, took hold partly because it recalls the 318 servants of Abraham in Genesis and is worth 318 in Greek numeration. The council was indeed held at Nicaea, with a real but uncertain number of bishops, and nothing indicates a count forbidden by Constantine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Greek term homoousios, affirmed by the Nicene Creed about the Son, mean?
choix: That the Son is a superior creature but distinct from the Father
That the Son is begotten, not made, of the same substance as the Father
That the Son and the Father share only some of their attributes
That the Son was created before all other creatures
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Creed affirms the Son as begotten, not made, of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father, and condemns the idea that there was a time when the Son did not exist.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who refuses to sign the final text of the Council of Nicaea in 325?
choix: Eusebius of Caesarea and two bishops from Egypt
Ambrose of Milan and his secretary
Emperor Constantine himself, not yet baptized
Arius and two bishops who remain loyal to him, Theonas and Secundus
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of all the participants, only three refuse to sign: Arius, a mere priest whose doctrine is condemned, and Theonas and Secundus, who remain loyal to him and are exiled with him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Emperor Constantine summon the Council of Nicaea in 325?
choix: To settle a territorial dispute between two eastern provinces
To officially crown a new patriarch of Constantinople
Because a theological disagreement over the nature of the Son was threatening the empire's civil peace
To answer a request from the Roman Senate to reform the calendar
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Constantine discovers that a theological question is dividing his eastern provinces to the point of threatening the civil peace he is trying to impose, and summons the bishops at his own expense.
